items.stem: What is the distance between two adjacent nodes on a stationary wave?
items.answer: Half a wavelength
items.markingKey: Nodes are λ/2 apart.

items.stem: Explain how a stationary wave is formed on a string fixed at both ends.
items.answer: A wave travels along the string and is reflected at the fixed ends; the incident and reflected waves (same speed, frequency and amplitude) travel in opposite directions and superpose, giving fixed nodes and antinodes.
items.markingKey: reflection at ends [1]; waves travelling in opposite directions with same f [1]; superposition forms nodes/antinodes [1] [3]

items.stem: State two differences between a stationary wave and a progressive wave.
items.answer: Stationary: no energy transfer along the wave; amplitude varies with position (nodes and antinodes); points in a loop are in phase. Progressive: transfers energy; constant amplitude; phase varies continuously.
items.markingKey: any two correct differences [2]

items.stem: A string of length 0.75 m is fixed at both ends and vibrated by a signal generator at 150 Hz. A stationary wave with 1 loop (antinode) is seen. Calculate the wavelength of the waves on the string.
items.markingKey: 1 loops = 1 × λ/2 = 0.75 m → λ = 2L/1 = 1.5 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A string of length 1.0 m is fixed at both ends and vibrated by a signal generator at 50 Hz. A stationary wave with 2 loops (antinodes) is seen. Calculate the speed of the waves on the string and the fundamental frequency.
items.answer: v = 50 m s⁻¹; f₁ = 25 Hz

items.stem: A string of length 1.2 m is fixed at both ends and vibrated by a signal generator at 60 Hz. A stationary wave with 1 loop (antinode) is seen. (a) Calculate the speed of the waves. (b) Calculate the frequency needed for one more loop. (c) State the number of nodes and the distance between adjacent antinodes. (d) Explain why points in adjacent loops are in antiphase.
items.answer: (a) 144 m s⁻¹ (b) 120 Hz (c) 2 nodes; 1.2 m (d) the displacement reverses across each node.
items.markingKey: (a) λ = 2.4 m, v = fλ = 144 m s⁻¹ [1] (b) f = (n + 1)v/2L = 120 Hz [1] (c) 2 nodes [1]; λ/2 = 1.2 m [1] (d) antiphase across a node [1] [5]

items.stem: In a school laboratory in Istanbul, a wire of length 0.80 m is stretched between two fixed points; its fundamental frequency is 75 Hz. (a) Calculate the speed of waves on the string. (b) Explain how the stationary wave is formed.
items.answer: (a) 120 m s⁻¹ (b) waves reflected at the fixed ends travel in opposite directions and superpose
items.markingKey: (a) v = fλ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 120 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) reflection [1]; superposition of opposite waves [1] [2]

items.stem: In a practical class in Manila, a wire of length 1.0 m is stretched between two fixed points; its fundamental frequency is 60 Hz. (a) Calculate the speed of waves on the string. (b) Calculate the frequency of the second harmonic. (c) Explain how the stationary wave is formed.
items.answer: (a) 120 m s⁻¹ (b) 120 Hz (c) waves reflected at the fixed ends travel in opposite directions and superpose
items.markingKey: (a) v = fλ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 120 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) 2f₁: 120 Hz [1] (c) reflection [1]; superposition of opposite waves [1] [2]

items.stem: A stationary wave is formed by …
options: two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions overlapping
a single wave reflecting at an angle
two waves of different frequency travelling in the same direction
items.answer: two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions overlapping
items.markingKey: Superposition of identical waves travelling in opposite directions.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A string fixed at both ends vibrates at its fundamental frequency. Its length L is related to the wavelength by … (b) State what is meant by a node.
items.answer: (a) L = λ/2 (b) A point on a stationary wave where the amplitude is always zero.
items.markingKey: (a) Nodes at each end, one antinode in the middle. (b) zero amplitude / no displacement [1]

items.stem: Describe how microwaves and a metal plate can be used to measure the wavelength of microwaves.
items.answer: Reflect microwaves from a metal plate to form a stationary wave; move a detector along the line and find positions of minimum signal (nodes); distance between adjacent nodes = λ/2; measure across several nodes.
items.markingKey: stationary wave by reflection [1]; locate nodes with detector [1]; node spacing = λ/2 over several nodes [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why there is always a node at the closed end of a resonance tube.
items.answer: Air molecules at the closed end cannot move (displacement must be zero), so there is a displacement node.
items.markingKey: air cannot move at closed end [1]; displacement node [1] [2]

items.stem: A tuning fork of frequency 320 Hz is held over a resonance tube closed at one end by water. The first resonance occurs when the air column is 25.8 cm long and the second when it is 77.3 cm long. Use the difference between the lengths to calculate the speed of sound.
items.answer: 330 m s⁻¹

items.stem: Microwaves reflected from a metal plate form a stationary wave. A detector moved along the line finds 7 consecutive minima spread over a distance of 9.6 cm. Calculate the wavelength and the frequency of the microwaves.
items.markingKey: 7 minima span 6 half-wavelengths [1]; λ = 2 × 9.6/6 = 3.2 cm [1]; f = c/λ = 9.38 × 10⁹ Hz [1] [3]

items.stem: A tuning fork of frequency 288 Hz is held over a resonance tube closed at one end by water. The first resonance occurs when the air column is 28.0 cm long and the second when it is 85.3 cm long. (a) Calculate the speed of sound. (b) Show that λ/4 is greater than the first length and explain why. (c) Explain why using the difference between the two lengths gives a more accurate result.
items.answer: (a) 330 m s⁻¹ (b) λ/4 = 28.6 cm > 28.0 cm because the antinode is slightly above the open end (end correction). (c) The end correction cancels in the difference.
items.markingKey: (a) λ/2 = difference [1]; v = 330 m s⁻¹ [1] (b) λ/4 = 28.6 cm [1]; end correction [1] (c) end correction cancels [1] [5]

items.stem: A string of length 1.2 m on an instrument made in Cairo has a fundamental frequency of 60 Hz. (a) Sketch the stationary wave at the fundamental frequency, labelling nodes N and antinodes A. (b) Calculate the wavelength of the fundamental.
items.answer: (a) one loop: N at each end, A in the middle (b) 2.4 m
items.markingKey: (a) N at ends [1]; A in middle [1] [2] (b) λ = 2L: 2.4 m [1]

items.stem: What is meant by diffraction?
options: The bouncing of a wave off a surface
The spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or around an edge
The change of direction of a wave entering a new medium
items.answer: The spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or around an edge
items.markingKey: Diffraction is spreading at gaps/edges.

items.stem: Describe how a ripple tank can be used to demonstrate diffraction.
items.answer: Plane waves from a vibrating bar pass through a gap between barriers; the pattern of wavefronts beyond the gap is viewed by shining light from above; vary the gap width to compare spreading.
items.markingKey: plane waves and gap [1]; observe wavefronts beyond gap [1]; vary gap [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why long-wave radio signals can be received in valleys where short-wave signals cannot.
items.answer: Long-wave radio has wavelengths comparable to hills, so it diffracts around them; shorter wavelengths diffract much less.
items.markingKey: long λ diffracts round hills [1]; short λ little diffraction [1] [2]

items.stem: Sound of frequency 256 Hz travels at 340 m s⁻¹ towards a doorway 0.90 m wide. Work out the wavelength of the sound.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 340/256 = 1.33 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Sound of frequency 256 Hz (speed 340 m s⁻¹) and green light (wavelength 550 nm) pass through an open doorway 0.90 m wide. Calculate the ratio gap/wavelength for each and use the values to explain why a person beyond the doorway, out of line of sight, can hear but not see a speaker.
items.answer: sound: 0.678; light: 1.6 × 10⁶. Sound diffracts significantly (gap ≈ λ); light hardly diffracts (gap ≫ λ).
items.markingKey: λ_sound = 1.33 m [1]; ratios 0.678 and 1.6 × 10⁶ [1]; significant diffraction only when gap ~ λ [1] [3]

items.stem: Plane water waves of wavelength 1.5 cm in a ripple tank in an AS Physics lesson in Madrid meet a barrier containing a gap. (a) Describe the wavefronts beyond a gap of width 12 cm. (b) State what is meant by diffraction. (c) Explain why the speed of the waves does not change on diffraction.
items.answer: (a) Mostly straight with slight curving at the edges, same wavelength (b) Spreading of a wave through a gap or around an obstacle. (c) The medium (depth of water) is unchanged; speed depends on the medium.
items.markingKey: (a) mostly straight [1]; edges curved [1] [2] (b) Spreading of a wave through a gap or around an obstacle [1] (c) The medium (depth of water) is unchanged; speed depends on the medium [1]

items.stem: Explain why a satellite dish must be accurately aligned with the satellite.
items.answer: The microwaves have a short wavelength compared with the dish size, so they diffract very little and form a narrow beam.
items.markingKey: λ ≪ dish size [1]; little diffraction / narrow beam [1] [2]

items.stem: Waves of water waves of wavelength 1.0 cm in a ripple tank pass through a gap 0.30 m wide. The wavelength is 0.010 m. Describe and explain the diffraction observed beyond the gap.
items.answer: Little diffraction: the gap is much wider than the wavelength, so the wavefronts pass through mostly straight with slight curving at the edges. The wavelength is unchanged.
items.markingKey: compares gap with wavelength [1]; correct extent of spreading [1]; wavelength unchanged [1] [3]

items.stem: Sound of frequency 680 Hz travels at 340 m s⁻¹ towards a doorway 1.0 m wide. Calculate the wavelength of the sound.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.50 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Plane water waves of wavelength 2.0 cm in a ripple tank in an AS Physics lesson in Istanbul meet a barrier containing a gap. (a) Describe the wavefronts beyond a gap of width 2.0 cm. (b) Suggest why harbour engineers prefer a wide entrance for calm water beside the entrance.
items.answer: (a) Strongly curved, nearly semicircular, same wavelength (b) Waves through a gap much wider than λ spread little into the sheltered areas.
items.markingKey: (a) semicircular spreading [1]; same λ [1] [2] (b) Waves through a gap much wider than λ spread little into the sheltered areas [1]

items.stem: A harbour model is built in a ripple tank; waves of wavelength 2.5 cm approach the harbour entrance. (a) Describe the wavefronts beyond a gap of width 2.5 cm. (b) Describe the wavefronts beyond a gap of width 20 cm. (c) Explain why the speed of the waves does not change on diffraction.
items.answer: (a) Strongly curved, nearly semicircular, same wavelength (b) Mostly straight with slight curving at the edges, same wavelength (c) The medium (depth of water) is unchanged; speed depends on the medium.
items.markingKey: (a) semicircular spreading [1]; same λ [1] [2] (b) mostly straight [1]; edges curved [1] [2] (c) The medium (depth of water) is unchanged; speed depends on the medium [1]

(b) State what is meant by diffraction. (c) Explain why the speed of the waves does not change on diffraction.
items.answer: (a) Strongly curved, nearly semicircular, same wavelength (b) Spreading of a wave through a gap or around an obstacle. (c) The medium (depth of water) is unchanged; speed depends on the medium.
items.markingKey: (a) semicircular spreading [1]; same λ [1] [2] (b) Spreading of a wave through a gap or around an obstacle [1] (c) The medium (depth of water) is unchanged; speed depends on the medium [1]

items.stem: What is meant by coherent sources?
options: Sources that have the same amplitude
Sources that are in the same place
Sources that have a constant phase difference
items.answer: Sources that have a constant phase difference
items.markingKey: Coherence: constant phase difference (and so same frequency).

items.stem: Explain why two separate lamps do not produce a visible interference pattern.
items.answer: They are not coherent: light is emitted in random bursts so the phase difference changes rapidly and randomly, and the pattern moves too fast to be seen.
items.markingKey: not coherent / phase difference not constant [1]; pattern changes too rapidly [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a bright fringe and a dark fringe are formed in Young's double-slit experiment.
items.answer: Light diffracts through each slit and the waves overlap; where the path difference is nλ the waves arrive in phase (constructive, bright); where it is (n + ½)λ they arrive in antiphase (destructive, dark).
items.markingKey: diffraction and overlap [1]; path difference nλ bright [1]; (n + ½)λ dark [1] [3]

items.stem: A helium-neon laser of wavelength 650 nm gives fringes 2.44 mm apart on a screen 3.0 m from two slits. Calculate the slit separation in mm.
items.markingKey: a = λD/x = 0.80 mm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A helium-neon laser illuminates two slits 0.80 mm apart. On a screen 2.5 m away, 11 bright fringes span 14.1 mm (centre to centre). Calculate the wavelength.
items.answer: 450 nm
items.markingKey: 11 fringes = 10 spacings: x = 1.41 mm [1]; λ = ax/D [1]; = 450 nm [1] [3]

items.stem: A helium-neon laser illuminates two slits 0.20 mm apart; the screen is 1.5 m away and 9 bright fringes span 35.3 mm. (a) Calculate the wavelength. (b) Explain why measuring across 9 fringes improves the result. (c) Predict the fringe separation if the screen is moved to 2.25 m and a source of wavelength 471 nm is used.
items.answer: (a) 589 nm (b) reduces the percentage uncertainty in x (c) 5.30 mm
items.markingKey: (a) x = 4.42 mm [1]; λ = ax/D = 589 nm [1] (b) larger distance measured, smaller % uncertainty [1] (c) x ∝ λD: × 1.5 × 0.8 [1]; = 5.30 mm [1] [5]

items.stem: Priya repeats Young's double-slit experiment with light of wavelength 650 nm, slit separation 0.40 mm and slit-screen distance 2.5 m. (a) State the path difference to the second bright fringe from the centre. (b) Describe the effect on the pattern of covering one slit. (c) Suggest why the fringe separation is measured across several fringes.
items.answer: (a) 2λ = 1300 nm (b) The interference fringes disappear; only a single-slit diffraction pattern (broad central band) remains. (c) It reduces the percentage uncertainty in x.
items.markingKey: (a) 2λ: 2λ = 1300 nm [1] (b) fringes disappear [1]; diffraction pattern remains [1] [2] (c) It reduces the percentage uncertainty in x [1]

items.stem: In a college physics laboratory in Jakarta, laser light of wavelength 650 nm passes through a double slit of separation 0.30 mm onto a screen 2.0 m away. (a) Calculate the fringe separation. (b) Explain what is meant by coherence and why the laser is suitable. (c) State the path difference to the second bright fringe from the centre.
items.answer: (a) 4.33 mm (b) Constant phase difference; light from the laser passing through both slits comes from the same wavefront. (c) 2λ = 1300 nm
items.markingKey: (a) x = λD/a (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.33 mm with unit [1] [2] (b) definition [1]; same source [1] [2] (c) 2λ: 2λ = 1300 nm [1]

items.stem: For constructive interference between waves from two coherent sources in phase, the path difference must be …
options: an odd number of half wavelengths
items.answer: a whole number of wavelengths
items.markingKey: Path difference = nλ.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which change makes the fringes in a double-slit experiment closer together? (b) In a double-slit experiment the slit separation is halved. The fringe separation …
items.answer: (a) Using blue light instead of red light (b) doubles
items.markingKey: (a) x ∝ λ; blue has a shorter wavelength. (b) x = λD/a ∝ 1/a.

items.stem: State the conditions needed for an observable two-source interference pattern.
items.answer: Coherent sources (constant phase difference), similar amplitudes, same type of wave (same polarisation for light), and waves must overlap.
items.markingKey: coherent [1]; similar amplitude / overlap [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the slits in a double-slit experiment must be narrow.
items.answer: Narrow slits diffract the light widely so that the waves from the two slits overlap over a wide region of the screen.
items.markingKey: narrow slits diffract more [1]; waves overlap [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the slits in a double-slit experiment must be narrow. (b) Explain how a bright fringe and a dark fringe are formed in Young's double-slit experiment.
items.answer: (a) Narrow slits diffract the light widely so that the waves from the two slits overlap over a wide region of the screen. (b) Light diffracts through each slit and the waves overlap; where the path difference is nλ the waves arrive in phase (constructive, bright); where it is (n + ½)λ they arrive in antiphase (destructive, dark).
items.markingKey: (a) narrow slits diffract more [1]; waves overlap [1] [2] (b) diffraction and overlap [1]; path difference nλ bright [1]; (n + ½)λ dark [1] [3]

items.stem: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit sound of frequency 850 Hz in phase (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). A microphone is 6.0 m from one speaker and 6.2 m from the other. Determine whether the microphone detects a loud or a quiet sound.
items.answer: Path difference = 0.200 m = 0.50λ, so destructive interference: quiet.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 0.40 m [1]; path difference = 0.200 m = 0.50λ [1]; correct conclusion [1] [3]

items.stem: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit sound of frequency 680 Hz in phase (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). A microphone is 3.0 m from one speaker and 3.75 m from the other. Determine whether the microphone detects a loud or a quiet sound.
items.answer: Path difference = 0.75 m = 1.5λ, so destructive interference: quiet.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 0.50 m [1]; path difference = 0.75 m = 1.5λ [1]; correct conclusion [1] [3]

items.stem: In an AS Physics lesson in Bangkok, laser light of wavelength 589 nm passes through a double slit of separation 0.40 mm onto a screen 1.5 m away. (a) State the path difference to the second bright fringe from the centre. (b) Describe the effect on the pattern of covering one slit. (c) Suggest why the fringe separation is measured across several fringes.
items.answer: (a) 2λ = 1180 nm (b) The interference fringes disappear; only a single-slit diffraction pattern (broad central band) remains. (c) It reduces the percentage uncertainty in x.

items.stem: A diffraction grating has 500 lines per mm. What is the line spacing d?
Explain why a diffraction grating gives a more accurate value of wavelength than a double-slit experiment.
items.answer: The maxima are sharp and bright and at large, easily measured angles, so the percentage uncertainty in θ (and so in λ) is small.
items.markingKey: sharp, bright maxima [1]; large angles, small % uncertainty [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a diffraction grating separates white light into a spectrum.
items.answer: Each wavelength has its maxima at a different angle (sin θ = nλ/d); longer wavelengths (red) are diffracted more, so the colours spread out in each order except the zero order.
items.markingKey: angle depends on λ [1]; red diffracted most, spectrum in each order [1] [2]

items.stem: Light from a green laser of wavelength 589 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 100 lines per mm. Calculate the angle of the order 2 maximum from the normal (in degrees).
items.markingKey: d = 1.00 × 10⁻⁵ m; sin θ = nλ/d = 0.118 = 6.77°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A narrow beam of light of wavelength 656 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 300 lines per mm. Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum and the highest order that can be observed.

Light containing wavelengths 436 nm and 476 nm falls normally on a grating with 500 lines per mm. (a) Calculate the first-order angles for each wavelength. (b) Calculate their angular separation. (c) Determine the total number of maxima seen for the 436 nm light.
items.markingKey: (a) d = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m [1]; sin θ = λ/d for each [1] (b) difference 1.18° [1] (c) n_max = 4 [1]; total = 2 × 4 + 1 = 9 [1] [5]

items.stem: An astronomer analyses light from a star with a grating of 600 lines per mm; the light spans 480 nm to 650 nm. (a) Calculate the line spacing of the grating. (b) Explain why the central maximum is white. (c) Explain why the grating gives sharper maxima than a double slit.
items.answer: (a) 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m (b) Zero path difference for all wavelengths. (c) Many slits: waves cancel except at exact angles where all are in phase.
items.markingKey: (a) d = 1/N: 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m [1] (b) Zero path difference for all wavelengths [1] (c) many slits [1]; cancellation away from exact angle [1] [2]

items.stem: An astronomer analyses light from a star with a grating of 300 lines per mm; the light spans 480 nm to 650 nm. (a) Calculate the angular width of the first-order spectrum. (b) Determine whether the second- and third-order spectra overlap.
items.markingKey: (a) angles 8.28° and 11.2° (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 2.97° with unit [1] [3] (b) compare 2 × 650 nm with 3 × 480 nm [1]; No [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which wavelength is diffracted through the largest angle in a given order? (b) In the zero-order maximum of a grating illuminated with white light, the light is …
items.answer: (a) red light (b) white
items.markingKey: (a) sin θ = nλ/d; red has the longest visible wavelength. (b) Path difference zero for all wavelengths.

items.stem: Explain why the zero-order maximum is the same colour as the source.
items.answer: At θ = 0 the path difference is zero for every wavelength, so all wavelengths interfere constructively at the same place.
items.markingKey: path difference zero for all λ [1]; all colours combine [1] [2]

items.stem: Monochromatic light passes through a grating onto a screen. The wavelength is tripled while the line spacing d stays the same. State and explain how the value of sin θ for the first-order maximum changes.
items.answer: The value of sin θ for the first-order maximum triples.
items.markingKey: Using d sin θ = nλ: value of sin θ for the first-order maximum ∝ wavelength; factor = 3.00 = 3.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Monochromatic light passes through a grating onto a screen. The wavelength is multiplied by 4 while the line spacing d stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the value of sin θ for the first-order maximum changes.
items.answer: The value of sin θ for the first-order maximum becomes 4 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using d sin θ = nλ: value of sin θ for the first-order maximum ∝ wavelength; factor = 4.00 = 4.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Sound of frequency 680 Hz travels at 340 m s⁻¹ towards a doorway 0.80 m wide. Determine the wavelength of the sound.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.50 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Plane water waves of wavelength 2.0 cm in a ripple tank in an AS Physics lesson in Istanbul meet a barrier containing a gap. (a) Describe the wavefronts beyond a gap of width 2.0 cm. (b) Describe the wavefronts beyond a gap of width 16 cm. (c) Explain why the speed of the waves does not change on diffraction.
items.answer: (a) Strongly curved, nearly semicircular, same wavelength (b) Mostly straight with slight curving at the edges, same wavelength (c) The medium (depth of water) is unchanged; speed depends on the medium.
items.markingKey: (a) semicircular spreading [1]; same λ [1] [2] (b) mostly straight [1]; edges curved [1] [2] (c) The medium (depth of water) is unchanged; speed depends on the medium [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is meant by coherent sources? (b) In a double-slit experiment, λ = 600 nm, slit separation a = 0.50 mm and D = 2.0 m. What is the fringe separation?
items.answer: (a) Sources that have a constant phase difference (b) 2.4 mm
items.markingKey: (a) Coherence: constant phase difference (and so same frequency). (b) x = λD/a = 600 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.0/0.50 × 10⁻³.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why two separate lamps do not produce a visible interference pattern. (b) Explain how a bright fringe and a dark fringe are formed in Young's double-slit experiment.
items.answer: (a) They are not coherent: light is emitted in random bursts so the phase difference changes rapidly and randomly, and the pattern moves too fast to be seen. (b) Light diffracts through each slit and the waves overlap; where the path difference is nλ the waves arrive in phase (constructive, bright); where it is (n + ½)λ they arrive in antiphase (destructive, dark).
items.markingKey: (a) not coherent / phase difference not constant [1]; pattern changes too rapidly [1] [2] (b) diffraction and overlap [1]; path difference nλ bright [1]; (n + ½)λ dark [1] [3]

items.stem: A sodium lamp with a filter of wavelength 700 nm gives fringes 3.50 mm apart on a screen 2.5 m from two slits. Calculate the slit separation in mm.
items.markingKey: a = λD/x = 0.50 mm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit sound of frequency 1700 Hz in phase (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). A microphone is 4.0 m from one speaker and 4.3 m from the other. Determine whether the microphone detects a loud or a quiet sound.
items.answer: Path difference = 0.300 m = 1.5λ, so destructive interference: quiet.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 0.20 m [1]; path difference = 0.300 m = 1.5λ [1]; correct conclusion [1] [3]

items.stem: In a school laboratory in Toronto, laser light of wavelength 589 nm passes through a double slit of separation 0.40 mm onto a screen 2.0 m away. (a) Calculate the fringe separation. (b) Describe the effect on the pattern of covering one slit.
items.answer: (a) 2.95 mm (b) The interference fringes disappear; only a single-slit diffraction pattern (broad central band) remains.
items.markingKey: (a) x = λD/a (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.95 mm with unit [1] [2] (b) fringes disappear [1]; diffraction pattern remains [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the zero-order maximum is the same colour as the source. (b) Explain how a diffraction grating separates white light into a spectrum.
items.answer: (a) At θ = 0 the path difference is zero for every wavelength, so all wavelengths interfere constructively at the same place. (b) Each wavelength has its maxima at a different angle (sin θ = nλ/d); longer wavelengths (red) are diffracted more, so the colours spread out in each order except the zero order.
items.markingKey: (a) path difference zero for all λ [1]; all colours combine [1] [2] (b) angle depends on λ [1]; red diffracted most, spectrum in each order [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the zero-order maximum is the same colour as the source. (b) Explain why a diffraction grating gives a more accurate value of wavelength than a double-slit experiment.
items.answer: (a) At θ = 0 the path difference is zero for every wavelength, so all wavelengths interfere constructively at the same place. (b) The maxima are sharp and bright and at large, easily measured angles, so the percentage uncertainty in θ (and so in λ) is small.
items.markingKey: (a) path difference zero for all λ [1]; all colours combine [1] [2] (b) sharp, bright maxima [1]; large angles, small % uncertainty [1] [2]

items.stem: Light from a laser of wavelength 486 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 600 lines per mm. Work out the angle of the order 2 maximum from the normal (in degrees).
items.markingKey: d = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m; sin θ = nλ/d = 0.583 = 35.7°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Monochromatic light from a discharge lamp of wavelength 546 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 300 lines per mm. Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum and the highest order that can be observed.

White light is shone normally onto a grating with 300 lines per mm in a school laboratory in Bogotá. The visible spectrum ranges from 450 nm to 700 nm. (a) Calculate the line spacing of the grating. (b) Explain why the central maximum is white. (c) Explain why the grating gives sharper maxima than a double slit.
items.answer: (a) 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m (b) Zero path difference for all wavelengths. (c) Many slits: waves cancel except at exact angles where all are in phase.
items.markingKey: (a) d = 1/N: 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m [1] (b) Zero path difference for all wavelengths [1] (c) many slits [1]; cancellation away from exact angle [1] [2]

items.stem: A string fixed at both ends vibrates at its fundamental frequency. Its length L is related to the wavelength by …
items.answer: L = λ/2
items.markingKey: Nodes at each end, one antinode in the middle.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State two differences between a stationary wave and a progressive wave. (b) Explain why there is always a node at the closed end of a resonance tube.
items.answer: (a) Stationary: no energy transfer along the wave; amplitude varies with position (nodes and antinodes); points in a loop are in phase. Progressive: transfers energy; constant amplitude; phase varies continuously. (b) Air molecules at the closed end cannot move (displacement must be zero), so there is a displacement node.
items.markingKey: (a) any two correct differences [2] (b) air cannot move at closed end [1]; displacement node [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) State two differences between a stationary wave and a progressive wave. (b) Explain how a stationary wave is formed on a string fixed at both ends.
items.answer: (a) Stationary: no energy transfer along the wave; amplitude varies with position (nodes and antinodes); points in a loop are in phase. Progressive: transfers energy; constant amplitude; phase varies continuously. (b) A wave travels along the string and is reflected at the fixed ends; the incident and reflected waves (same speed, frequency and amplitude) travel in opposite directions and superpose, giving fixed nodes and antinodes.
items.markingKey: (a) any two correct differences [2] (b) reflection at ends [1]; waves travelling in opposite directions with same f [1]; superposition forms nodes/antinodes [1] [3]

items.stem: A string of length 1.0 m is fixed at both ends and vibrated by a signal generator at 100 Hz. A stationary wave with 2 loops (antinodes) is seen. Determine the wavelength of the waves on the string.
items.markingKey: 2 loops = 2 × λ/2 = 1.0 m → λ = 2L/2 = 1.0 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A string of length 0.60 m is fixed at both ends and vibrated by a signal generator at 100 Hz. A stationary wave with 1 loop (antinode) is seen. Calculate the speed of the waves on the string and the fundamental frequency.
items.answer: v = 120 m s⁻¹; f₁ = 100 Hz

items.stem: In a school laboratory in Jakarta, a wire of length 0.80 m is stretched between two fixed points; its fundamental frequency is 90 Hz. (a) Sketch the stationary wave at the fundamental frequency, labelling nodes N and antinodes A. (b) Calculate the speed of waves on the string. (c) Calculate the frequency of the second harmonic. (d) State the phase difference between points on either side of a node.
items.answer: (a) one loop: N at each end, A in the middle (b) 144 m s⁻¹ (c) 180 Hz (d) 180° (π rad)
items.markingKey: (a) N at ends [1]; A in middle [1] [2] (b) v = fλ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 144 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (c) 2f₁: 180 Hz [1] (d) antiphase: 180° (π rad) [1]

items.stem: When a wave diffracts through a gap, its wavelength …
items.answer: stays the same
items.markingKey: Speed and frequency unchanged, so λ unchanged.

items.stem: Waves of water waves of wavelength 2.0 cm in a ripple tank pass through a gap 0.016 m wide. The wavelength is 0.020 m. Describe and explain the diffraction observed beyond the gap.
items.answer: Strong diffraction: the gap is similar to the wavelength, so the waves spread out into nearly circular wavefronts. The wavelength is unchanged.
items.markingKey: compares gap with wavelength [1]; correct extent of spreading [1]; wavelength unchanged [1] [3]

items.stem: Sound of frequency 340 Hz travels at 340 m s⁻¹ towards a doorway 1.0 m wide. Determine the wavelength of the sound.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 340/340 = 1.0 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A harbour model is built in a ripple tank; waves of wavelength 1.5 cm approach the harbour entrance. (a) Describe the wavefronts beyond a gap of width 12 cm. (b) State what is meant by diffraction. (c) Explain why the speed of the waves does not change on diffraction. (d) Suggest why harbour engineers prefer a wide entrance for calm water beside the entrance.
items.answer: (a) Mostly straight with slight curving at the edges, same wavelength (b) Spreading of a wave through a gap or around an obstacle. (c) The medium (depth of water) is unchanged; speed depends on the medium. (d) Waves through a gap much wider than λ spread little into the sheltered areas.
items.markingKey: (a) mostly straight [1]; edges curved [1] [2] (b) Spreading of a wave through a gap or around an obstacle [1] (c) The medium (depth of water) is unchanged; speed depends on the medium [1] (d) Waves through a gap much wider than λ spread little into the sheltered areas [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which change makes the fringes in a double-slit experiment closer together? (b) For constructive interference between waves from two coherent sources in phase, the path difference must be …
items.answer: (a) Using blue light instead of red light (b) a whole number of wavelengths
items.markingKey: (a) x ∝ λ; blue has a shorter wavelength. (b) Path difference = nλ.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) State the conditions needed for an observable two-source interference pattern. (b) Explain why two separate lamps do not produce a visible interference pattern.
items.answer: (a) Coherent sources (constant phase difference), similar amplitudes, same type of wave (same polarisation for light), and waves must overlap. (b) They are not coherent: light is emitted in random bursts so the phase difference changes rapidly and randomly, and the pattern moves too fast to be seen.
items.markingKey: (a) coherent [1]; similar amplitude / overlap [1] [2] (b) not coherent / phase difference not constant [1]; pattern changes too rapidly [1] [2]

items.stem: A helium-neon laser of wavelength 500 nm illuminates two slits 0.25 mm apart. Fringes form on a screen 3.0 m away. Determine the fringe separation.
items.markingKey: x = λD/a = 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ × 3.0/2.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 6.00 mm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit sound of frequency 500 Hz in phase (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). A microphone is 3.0 m from one speaker and 3.34 m from the other. Determine whether the microphone detects a loud or a quiet sound.
items.answer: Path difference = 0.340 m = 0.50λ, so destructive interference: quiet.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 0.68 m [1]; path difference = 0.340 m = 0.50λ [1]; correct conclusion [1] [3]

items.answer: (a) 3.96 mm (b) The interference fringes disappear; only a single-slit diffraction pattern (broad central band) remains.

items.stem: Light is incident normally on a diffraction grating. The line spacing d is doubled while the wavelength stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the value of sin θ for the first-order maximum changes.
items.answer: The value of sin θ for the first-order maximum halves.
items.markingKey: Using d sin θ = nλ: value of sin θ for the first-order maximum ∝ line spacing d^-1.00; factor = 2.00^-1.00 = 0.500. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A narrow beam of light of wavelength 589 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 300 lines per mm. Determine the angle of the order 3 maximum from the normal (in degrees).
items.markingKey: d = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m; sin θ = nλ/d = 0.530 = 32.0°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A student measures the angle between the two order-2 maxima (on either side of the centre) produced by a grating with 500 lines per mm as 72.2°. Calculate the wavelength of the light.
items.answer: 589 nm

items.stem: An astronomer analyses light from a star with a grating of 300 lines per mm; the light spans 450 nm to 700 nm. (a) Calculate the angular width of the first-order spectrum. (b) Explain why the central maximum is white.
items.answer: (a) 4.36° (b) Zero path difference for all wavelengths.
